title: How To Turn Around Difficult Students (Part 3) https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/03/13/difficult-students-turning-them-around-part-3/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Closing his three-part series, Linsin focuses on how teachers should communicate with difficult students to build genuine influence over their behavior. He identifies two counterproductive habits: reacting to misbehavior with frustration, scolding, or threats, which breeds dislike and destroys influence; and over-praising expected behavior, which signals that the student can't control themselves like everyone else. His recommended approach centers on four guidelines: give difficult students no more attention than any other student, avoid causing friction through scolding or berating, deliberately develop a friendly relationship built around shared interests rather than behavior talk, and make room for genuine fun together. Linsin frames influence—being liked and trusted—as the true lever for lasting change, arguing that a difficult student who likes and trusts a teacher will want to behave, whereas one who doesn't will resist no matter what consequences are imposed.
points: Two counterproductive habits undermine influence with difficult students: reacting in frustration and over-praising expected behavior.
Give difficult students no more individual attention than any other student, cutting off excessive lectures, reminders, and warnings.
Avoid friction-causing reactions like scolding or berating, since disliking the teacher destroys any hope of influence.
Deliberately build a friendly relationship around shared interests rather than repeated conversations about behavior.
Genuine influence—being liked and trusted—is what makes a difficult student want to behave, more than consequences alone.
quotes: This third and final part of this series is about communicating with difficult students in a way that will compel them to behave the way you want them to.

In dealing with difficult students, teachers become frustrated and react by scolding, yelling, and threatening. True, these methods may suppress behavior in the short term, but they do nothing to improve behavior over time.

When difficult students do something correctly, teachers tend to praise too much or too demonstratively. They hug, cheer, high-five, celebrate, and give rewards and prizes—often for expected behavior.
Your goal with difficult students should be to build influence with them. When a student likes and trusts you, they’ll want to behave in a way that pleases you.
A good rule of thumb is to not spend any more time on them than the rest of your students.
It’s a myth that having fun somehow causes students to misbehave. The opposite is true.
If you build influence with difficult students, and you’re committed to holding them accountable when they misbehave, you can completely and unalterably turn them around.
